scripts.opening:opening:
[measured] Romanesque style walk.

[short pause] A winter afternoon, 1904, the elms bare and the stone showing. In the 1880s one architect from Boston, Henry Hobson Richardson, made heavy stone fashionable again: rough-faced blocks, deep round arches like a castle gate, and towers. [short pause] Chicago loved it, and for a few years its rich wanted fortresses.

[short pause] Four houses on foot, 1800 to 2110 Prairie. Look for rock-faced stone, arches that seem to sink into the wall, and turrets.

[short pause] Start with the house that started it, the one its neighbours hated.
scripts.stop:glessner: [measured] 1800 Prairie, Glessner House, the street's Richardsonian Romanesque original. [short pause] Its street walls are brick faced with alternate six- and eight-inch sheets of granite, cut deeper at the openings so the whole wall looks solid stone, under a roof of unglazed red tiles. [short pause] Richardson, all 370 pounds of him, held that the windows of a city house were 'not to look out of', so the street side is nearly blank and the family rooms open on a courtyard behind. [short pause] George Pullman, across the corner, complained about 'that thing staring me in the face'. [short pause] Across the avenue and a little south, the style caught on.
scripts.stop:ames: [measured] 1811 Prairie, the Coleman house of 1886, by Cobb and Frost, who were well known for their Romanesque work. [short pause] This front is rough-faced brown sandstone. The 1888 plate shows the style's signature: a deep round arch on clustered columns over a broad stair, and a corbelled oriel bulging out above it, like a lookout on a castle wall. [short pause] Notice that the arch is the door: in this style, the entrance is a tunnel into the stone. [short pause] Walk south past Twentieth Street for two smaller fortresses.
scripts.stop:r2011: [measured] 2011 Prairie, a neighbour of the Mayer house. [short pause] The district register reads it as Romanesque: a rough ashlar front, a round-arched entrance, and a rounded corner turret under a conical cap. A turret on a city lot is pure theatre: a castle tower on a town house. [short pause] Across the avenue and a block on, the last of the four squeezes the style onto one narrow lot.
scripts.stop:rees: [measured] 2110 Prairie, Harriet Rees's narrow house, read by the district register as Cobb and Frost's work of 1888 and as Romanesque: a limestone front under a tall gable facing the avenue. [short pause] Two years after their Coleman house, the same architects did the style in pale stone for a woman's house. [short pause] Compare the two: same firm, opposite colour.
scripts.ending:finish:
[measured] End of the Romanesque walk. Rough stone, round arches, towers: the fashion of the 1880s on this street.

[short pause] But Richardson's fortress outlived nearly every house around it, and it is still standing. Walk back up to Eighteenth Street and look at it once more in the winter light.
